derivations.claim: The surface $S$ is Lebesgue-null in $\Omega$: by [L3] the finitely many regular charts $X_j:V_j\to S$ cover $S$, each image $X_j(V_j)$ is null in $\mathbb R^3$ by [L5] because $X_j$ is a $C^1$ map from the lower-dimensional open set $V_j\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, and a finite union of null sets is null by [L5]. Consequently, for $F\in\{B,D\}$ the distributional time derivative of the regular distribution of $F$ is the regular distribution of the piecewise classical time derivative: fix a test $\psi$ with support in a compact cylinder $\overline Q\times J\subseteq U$, so that $\langle\partial_tF,\psi\rangle=-\int_U F\partial_t\psi$; by [L8] applied after Fubini, this iterated integral equals $-\int_Q\int_JF(x,t)\partial_t\psi(x,t)\,dt\,dx$, and for every $x\in\Omega\setminus S$ the inner integrand is $C^1$ in $t$ with $\psi(x,\cdot)$ compactly supported in $J$, so [L8] gives $\int_JF(x,t)\partial_t\psi(x,t)\,dt=-\int_J\partial_tF(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dt$; since $S$ is null, replacing the outer integral over $\Omega\setminus S$ by one over $\Omega$ changes nothing, so $\langle\partial_tF,\psi\rangle=\int_U\{\partial_tF\}\psi$ for every test $\psi$, where $\{\partial_tF\}$ is locally bounded by the joint one-sided $C^1$ extension hypothesis.

By [L1], applied to $D$, $B$, $E$, $H$ (each is $C^1$ on $\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$ with one-sided $C^1$ traces under the joint extension hypothesis), the four spatial identities $\operatorname{div}D=\{\operatorname{div}D\}+n\cdot[D]\delta_S$, $\operatorname{div}B=\{\operatorname{div}B\}+n\cdot[B]\delta_S$, $\operatorname{curl}E=\{\operatorname{curl}E\}+n\times[E]\delta_S$ and $\operatorname{curl}H=\{\operatorname{curl}H\}+n\times[H]\delta_S$ hold as distributions on $U$ under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, with the piecewise fields locally bounded near $S$.

[Coefficient extraction] Let $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and let $a$ be measurable and locally integrable on $S\times I$ for $dS\,dt$, with $u_g+a\delta_S=0$. Every smooth test supported away from $S\times I$ has zero sheet pairing; the fundamental lemma [L7] applied on that open complement therefore gives $g=0$ almost everywhere there. Since $S$ is null by step 1.1, Fubini [L8] makes $S\times I$ null locally in spacetime, so $g=0$ almost everywhere on $U$. Thus $\int_{S\times I}a\psi\,dS\,dt=0$ for every ambient smooth compact test $\psi$. In a sufficiently small rigid graph chart write $X(y)=(y,h(y))$, with a product box $V\times(z_-,z_+)\times J$ contained in the ambient chart/time domain. Shrink $V$ and the height interval so the graph over $V$ stays in a closed subinterval inside $(z_-,z_+)$. For any $\eta\in C_c^\infty(V\times J)$ choose $\beta\in C_c^\infty((z_-,z_+))$ equal to $1$ on that graph-height interval by [L6], and take the ambient smooth test $\psi(y,z,t)=\eta(y,t)\beta(z)$, transported by the rigid motion and extended by zero. This test uses no composition with the merely $C^2$ graph function; its restriction to $S$ is $\eta$. The chart formula [L3] gives $\int_{V\times J}(a\circ X)(y,t)J_X(y)\eta(y,t)\,dy\,dt=0$. By [L7], $(a\circ X)J_X=0$ almost everywhere; positivity and continuity of $J_X$ give $a=0$ surface-time almost everywhere. Such small boxes cover every chart, so the conclusion holds on $S\times I$. In the joint branch $a\circ X$ is continuous; if it were nonzero at one point it would stay bounded away from zero on a nonempty parameter-time box of positive Lebesgue measure, contradicting the almost-everywhere conclusion. Thus $a=0$ pointwise in that branch.

Substituting the spatial identities of step 1.2 and the temporal identity of step 1.1 into the assumed identities [A1] gives four distributional identities of the form $u_g+a\delta_S=0$ with locally integrable volume parts: $u_{\{\operatorname{div}D\}-\rho_v}+(n\cdot[D]-\sigma_f)\delta_S=0$, $u_{\{\operatorname{div}B\}}+n\cdot[B]\delta_S=0$, $u_{\{\operatorname{curl}E\}+\{\partial_tB\}}+n\times[E]\delta_S=0$ and $u_{\{\operatorname{curl}H\}-J_v-\{\partial_tD\}}+(n\times[H]-K_f)\delta_S=0$; the sums are locally integrable because the piecewise fields and $J_v,\rho_v$ are locally integrable and the piecewise derivatives are locally bounded near $S$ (joint branch) or assumed locally integrable (weak-trace branch), and the sheet coefficients are the stated one-sided jump densities, continuous in the joint branch.

Apply step 2.1 to each of the four identities of step 2.2: the four coefficients $n\cdot[D]-\sigma_f$, $n\cdot[B]$, $n\times[E]$ and $n\times[H]-K_f$ vanish $dS\,dt$-almost everywhere, and in the joint branch they are continuous on $S\times I$ (one-sided traces of locally uniformly continuous extensions), hence vanish pointwise on $S\times I$; this proves $n\cdot[D]=\sigma_f$, $n\cdot[B]=0$, $n\times[E]=0$ and $n\times[H]=K_f$ pointwise, equivalently $\sigma_f=n\cdot[D]$ and $K_f=n\times[H]$, and the inner and cross products are those of the one-sided traces written in the frame basis of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]. In the weak-trace branch the four coefficients vanish $dS\,dt$-almost everywhere; since the traces are spatially continuous at each fixed time, vanishing on a set of full $dS$-measure for almost every $t$ upgrades to every $x\in S$ for almost every $t$, and if the jump densities are additionally jointly continuous, to every $(x,t)\in S\times I$; the four identities hold as identities of sheet distributions in both branches, and all statements are conditional on the assumed distributional equations [A1] with $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ carried from step 1.2.

boundaries.evidence: Statement: S is a fixed compact embedded hypersurface with chosen normal; the identities are asserted for that interface, and if S were empty every claim is vacuous (no sheet, no jump). No nonemptiness or existence of a field configuration is asserted, as step 3.1 records.

Steps 1.1-3.1: with E=B=D=H=0, sigma_f=0, K_f=0 and rho_v=J_v=0 the hypothesis [A1] holds (all distributions zero) and the conclusions reduce to 0=0; the zero coefficient case a=0 is exactly what step 2.1 produces, and the extraction is valid for the zero L^1 functions.

Statement and step 3.1: there is exactly one interface S and three spatial dimensions; the inner and cross products are those of R^3 (L2 and the frame conventions). The scalar normal components and the tangential vector components are the only cases that occur; no higher-codimension or multi-sheet case is claimed.

Steps 2.1 and 3.1: the inhomogeneous cases sigma_f nonzero and K_f nonzero are retained (no silent vanishing), the tangential electric jump vanishes for every pair of one-sided traces including coincident traces, and no nondegeneracy of the fields, of the interface metric or of the coefficients is assumed. Degenerate configurations are covered by the same a=0 extraction.

Statement: S is a compact embedded hypersurface without boundary and I is open, so the distributional lemma L1 applies away from the (empty) edge of S and no endpoint or boundary term arises; the nullity and chart arguments of step 1.1 use the finitely many charts covering the whole compact S.

Countable Choice is assumed and used exactly where needed: the interface lemma of step 1.2 assumes AC_omega (L1), the surface measure and regular-distribution interfaces of steps 1.1 and 2.1 assume AC_omega (L3, L4), and the nullity proposition of step 1.1 assumes countable choice (L5). No uncountable choice or selection of charts is hidden; the finite chart family is part of the surface-integral convention.
Step 3.1: from the four jump identities the sheet densities are read off as sigma_f = n.[D] and K_f = n x [H]; these are the same identities, so the forward direction is immediate.

Step 3.1: conversely the equalities sigma_f = n.[D] and K_f = n x [H] written in the two directions are literal identities after substituting the extracted pointwise relations for n.[D] and n x [H]; the 'equivalently' clause is therefore the same statement and needs no separate argument.

derivations.claim: Let $F\in\{E,B,D,H\}$ and let $\psi$ be a test function supported in a compact cylinder of $U$. For fixed $(x,y,t)$ with $z\ne0$ the map $z\mapsto F(x,y,z,t)$ is $C^1$ on each open half-line and $\psi$ has compact support in $z$; applying [L1] on $(-\infty,0)$ and on $(0,\infty)$ and summing gives $\int_{\mathbb R}F\,\partial_z\psi\,dz=-[F](x,y,0,t)\,\psi(x,y,0,t)-\int_{\mathbb R}\{\partial_zF\}\psi\,dz$, because the outer boundary terms vanish by compact support; integrating over $x,y,t$ by [L2], with the plane $\{z=0\}$ null by [L4] so that the split into the two half-spaces is exact, gives $\langle\partial_zF,\psi\rangle=\int_U\{\partial_zF\}\psi+\langle[F]\delta_S,\psi\rangle$ componentwise, i.e. $\operatorname{div}F=\{\operatorname{div}F\}+e_z\cdot[F]\,\delta_S$ and $\operatorname{curl}F=\{\operatorname{curl}F\}+e_z\times[F]\,\delta_S$ by [L6], the tangential derivatives contributing no sheet term.

The same per-line integration by parts in $t$, with $\psi$ of compact $t$-support and the plane stationary and null by [L4], gives $\langle\partial_tF,\psi\rangle=\int_U\{\partial_tF\}\psi$ for every test $\psi$: time differentiation at the fixed plane contributes no sheet term, and the piecewise derivatives are locally bounded by the joint one-sided $C^1$ hypothesis.

Substituting the spatial identities of step 1.1 and the temporal identity of step 1.2 into the assumed equations [A2] gives four distributional identities of the form $u_g+a\delta_S=0$ on the local region, with locally integrable volume parts $g$: $u_{\{\operatorname{div}D\}-\rho_v}+(n\cdot[D]-\sigma_f)\delta_S=0$, $u_{\{\operatorname{div}B\}}+n\cdot[B]\delta_S=0$, $u_{\{\operatorname{curl}E\}+\{\partial_tB\}}+n\times[E]\delta_S=0$ and $u_{\{\operatorname{curl}H\}-J_v-\{\partial_tD\}}+n\times[H]\delta_S=0$, where the two half-space fields are $C^1$ with locally bounded derivatives and $\rho_v,J_v$ are locally integrable.

[Coefficient extraction] Let $b\in C_c^\infty((-1,1))$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R$, with $b(0)=1$, $0\le b\le1$ [L3] and put $\psi_h:=\psi\,b(z/h)$ for a test $\psi$; testing an identity $u_g+a\delta_S=0$ of step 2.1 with $\psi_h$ gives $0=\int_Ug\psi_h+\int_{\{z=0\}}a\psi_h$, whose second term tends to $\int_{\{z=0\}}a\psi$ because $b(z/h)\to b(0)=1$ everywhere on the plane and the integrands are dominated by $|a\psi|$ on the compactly supported part of the plane, while the first term tends to $0$ because $|\int_Ug\psi_h|\le\int_U|g\psi|\mathbf 1_{\{|z|\le h\}}$ with integrands converging to $0$ almost everywhere, dominated by the integrable $|g\psi|$, the exceptional set $\{z=0\}$ being null [L4]. Hence $\int_{\{z=0\}}a\psi=0$ for every test $\psi$; taking $\psi(x,y,z,t)=\eta(x,y,t)\beta(z)$ with $\eta$ a test function in the tangential/time variables and $\beta$ a cutoff with $\beta(0)=1$ reduces this to $\int a(x,y,0,t)\eta(x,y,t)\,dx\,dy\,dt=0$ for every $\eta$, so the continuous function $(x,y,t)\mapsto a(x,y,0,t)$ vanishes identically by [L5]. All four coefficients of step 2.1 therefore vanish pointwise on the plane.

Applying step 3.1 and the constitutive relations [A1]: (a) $n\times[E]=0$, so the tangential parts agree, $E_{2t}=E_{1t}$; (b) $n\cdot[D]=\sigma_f$ with $D_j=\varepsilon_jE_j$ on the two sides gives $\varepsilon_2E_{2n}-\varepsilon_1E_{1n}=\sigma_f$ and, since $\varepsilon_2>0$, $E_{2n}=(\varepsilon_1/\varepsilon_2)E_{1n}+\sigma_f/\varepsilon_2$; (c) if $\sigma_f=0$ the previous identity reads $\varepsilon_2E_{2n}=\varepsilon_1E_{1n}$, so $E_{2n}=(\varepsilon_1/\varepsilon_2)E_{1n}$ has the same sign as $E_{1n}$ and vanishes with it, and $E_{2n}=E_{1n}$ holds if and only if $(\varepsilon_1-\varepsilon_2)E_{1n}=0$, i.e. when $E_{1n}=0$ or $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2$; (d) $n\cdot[B]=0$ and $n\times[H]=0$, and in the nonmagnetic case $H=\mu_0^{-1}B$ on both sides the two identities give $[B_n]=0$ and $[B_t]=0$, hence $B_{2n}=B_{1n}$ and $B_{2t}=B_{1t}$ by the decomposition of [L6]. The scope (e) holds: the computation uses only the assumed local equations and the declared linear branch, asserts no global configuration, no existence, no further constitutive law and no empirical claim.

boundaries.evidence: Example and step 3.1: if a coefficient vanished identically the extraction still holds; the empty-support case of the test pairing is zero, and no nonemptiness of the plane's portion inside a compact cylinder or of the source support is assumed.

Steps 4.1: sigma_f=0 is treated explicitly in (c) (the normal relation becomes eps2 E_2n = eps1 E_1n, with common signs), the zero fields satisfy all four identities, and the zero free sheet current K_f=0 is the case used in (d).

Example and step 4.1: one planar interface, three spatial dimensions and the isotropic scalar permittivities eps1, eps2 are the case at hand; the normal/tangential decomposition against the single unit normal e_z gives one normal and two tangential components, and no anisotropic or multilayer case is claimed.

Step 4.1: the degenerate equal-permittivity case eps1=eps2 is retained (E_2n=E_1n for every E_1n) and distinguished from the generic case; the case E_1n=0 is retained as the other way the equality E_2n=E_1n can hold; no invertibility beyond eps2>0 is assumed.

Steps 1.1-3.1: all pairings are over compact test supports inside the local laboratory region, so no asymptotic or global endpoint of the noncompact plane arises; the fixed-volume/far-field endpoint case is not asserted, and the time derivative carries no sheet term because the interface is stationary.

Countable Choice is assumed for the distributional and surface-measure interfaces as in the Example; it is used in the sheet pairing and in the extraction through the measure-theoretic suppliers L2 and L4, while the per-line integration by parts and the final algebra of step 4.1 are choice-free.
Step 4.1(c): if E_2n=E_1n and sigma_f=0, then (eps1-eps2)E_1n=eps2E_2n-eps2E_1n=eps2(E_2n-E_1n)=0, so either E_1n=0 or eps1=eps2; the forward direction of the stated equivalence is this computation.

Step 4.1(c): conversely, if E_1n=0 then eps2E_2n=eps1E_1n=0 gives E_2n=0=E_1n, and if eps1=eps2 then eps2E_2n=eps1E_1n=eps2E_1n with eps2>0 gives E_2n=E_1n; the reverse direction is the other half of the same equivalence.
